articles.title: Watch: Alaskan flying team airdrops Thanksgiving turkeys to remote communities
articles.summary: For the last few years, the "turkey bombers" have taken to the skies for the benefit of residents in off-grid communities.
articles.body:
For the last few years, "turkey bombers" Esther Keim and Heidi Hastings have taken to the skies to airdrop Thanksgiving turkeys to residents in off-grid communities in south-central Alaska.

Hastings pilots the plane while her best friend Keim drops the turkeys out the plane window, delivering to families who may not otherwise get one of the birds, since they are cut off by snow and ice.

articles.title: Anthropic will face a class-action lawsuit from US authors
articles.summary: A California federal judge ruled Thursday that three authors suing Anthropic over copyright infringement can bring a class action lawsuit representing all U.S. writers whose work was allegedly downloaded from libraries of pirated works.
articles.body: A California federal judge ruled Thursday that three authors suing Anthropic over copyright infringement can bring a class action lawsuit representing all US writers whose work was allegedly downloaded from libraries of pirated works. The filing alleges that Anthropic, the Amazon-backed OpenAI competitor behind the chatbot Claude, “violated the Copyright Act by doing Napster-style downloading of millions of works.” It alleges that the company downloaded as many as seven million copies of books from libraries of pirated works. The new ruling impacts a lawsuit filed last August by authors Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber, and Kirk Wallace Johnson, who alleged that Anthropic had “built a multibillion-dollar business by stealing hundreds of thousands of copyrighted books.” Late last month, a federal judge sided with Anthropic to rule that training its AI models on legally-purchased books was fair use but noted the company would need to face a separate trial for using allegedly pirated books. It also follows the lawsuit Reddit filed against Anthropic last month, claiming that the AI company’s bots had accessed Reddit more than 100,000 times since last July, after Anthropic had said it blocked them from doing so. The authors’ lawsuit is part of a growing trend of media outlets, platforms, companies, and creatives either suing AI companies over copyright infringement — for instance, Universal Music’s 2023 lawsuit against Anthropic over “systematic and widespread infringement of their copyrighted song lyrics” — or partnering up with them to willingly provide AI training data in order to get a slice of the profits.

articles.title: Anthropic to pay $1.5 billion to authors in landmark AI settlement
articles.summary: A settlement between Anthropic and authors over books used to train its AI would pay out “at least” $1.5 billion to resolve a class-action copyright lawsuit.
articles.body: In what’s potentially the first major payout to creatives whose work was used to train AI systems, Anthropic has reached an agreement to pay “at least” a staggering $1.5 billion, plus interest, to authors to settle its class-action lawsuit. The amount breaks down to smaller payouts expected to be approximately $3,000 per book or work. Lawyers for the plaintiffs said it’s “believed to be the largest publicly reported recovery in the history of US copyright litigation.” “This result is nothing short of remarkable,” the legal filing states. The settlement is subject to court approval, and a hearing will take place on September 8th. According to a press release, the final amount could be higher, in that approximately 500,000 works will likely be paid out, but if the total is higher than that, Anthropic will pay an additional $3,000 per work, and it all depends on the number of claims submitted. As part of the settlement, Anthropic must also destroy the original files it downloaded and any copies. “The settlement only releases claims based on past acts – it does not give Anthropic a license or permission for future AI training and it does not release any claims that arise after August 25, 2025,” the release stated. The landmark decision is part of a year-long saga. In August 2024, three authors — Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber, and Kirk Wallace Johnson — alleged that Anthropic had “built a multibillion-dollar business by stealing hundreds of thousands of copyrighted books.” Over the summer, a federal judge handed Anthropic a small win, ruling that the company was within its legal rights to train its AI models on legally purchased books. But the judge also said that Anthropic would need to face a separate trial for its alleged use of pirated books. In July, a California federal judge ruled that the authors could bring a class action lawsuit representing all US writers whose work allegedly came from libraries of pirated books downloaded by Anthropic. And late last month, Anthropic said it had settled the class action lawsuit — but we didn’t know the terms until now. “In June, the District Court issued a landmark ruling on AI development and copyright law, finding that Anthropic’s approach to training AI models constitutes fair use,” Aparna Sridhar, Anthropic’s deputy general counsel, told The Verge in a statement. “Today’s settlement, if approved, will resolve the plaintiffs’ remaining legacy claims. We remain committed to developing safe AI systems that help people and organizations extend their capabilities, advance scientific discovery, and solve complex problems.” The settlement is especially noteworthy during a time of mounting lawsuits against AI companies over copyright infringement from media outlets, platforms, creatives, and companies — and, at the same time, an increasing number of partnerships with those same AI companies from companies and media outlets willing to provide data to train AI systems in order to get a piece of the pie. It’s not the only legal action Anthropic has faced in recent years. This summer, Reddit filed suit against Anthropic, claiming that the AI company’s bots had accessed Reddit more than 100,000 times since July 2024, after Anthropic had said it blocked them from doing so. And in 2023, Universal Music sued Anthropic over “systematic and widespread infringement of their copyrighted song lyrics.” For this case, authors and rightsholders may visit AnthropicCopyrightSettlement.com, the release stated, a website that “which gives potential class members an option to provide contact information to Class Counsel.” “In the coming weeks, and if the court preliminarily approves the settlement, the website will provide to find a full and easily searchable listing of all works covered by the settlement and information for class members about their options and rights regarding the settlement,” the release said. articles.title: Canonical lays out a plan for AI in Ubuntu Linux
articles.summary: Ubuntu developer Canonical has announced plans to start adding AI features to the popular Linux distribution over the next year.
articles.body: One of the most popular Linux distributions is about to get an influx of AI features. As reported by Phoronix, Jon Seager, VP of engineering at Ubuntu developer Canonical, shared a blog post on Monday detailing plans to add AI features to the Linux distro over the next year. As the post states, the AI features “will come in two forms: first as a means of enhancing existing OS functionality with AI models in the background, and latterly in the form of ‘AI native’ features and workflows for those who want them.” These features will range from accessibility tools like improved speech-to-text and text-to-speech to agentic AI features for tasks like troubleshooting or personal automation. According to Seager, Canonical will be prioritizing model transparency and local inference when adding these AI features. Behind the scenes, Canonical is also encouraging its engineers to use AI more, but Seager noted that “I will not be measuring people at Canonical by how much they use AI, but rather continue to measure them on how well they deliver.” Seager goes on to add that AI features could potentially help new users navigate the “famously fragmented” Linux desktop ecosystem: “If we’re careful about how we employ LLMs in a system context, they could demystify the capabilities of a modern Linux workstation and bring them to a much wider audience.”

articles.title: Anthropic’s $1.5 billion book piracy settlement approved by judge
articles.summary: A federal judge has approved Anthropic’s $1.5 billion settlement with authors who accused it of stealing their copyrighted books.
articles.body: A federal judge has signed off on Anthropic’s $1.5 billion class action settlement with authors who accused the company of training its AI models on copyrighted books, as reported earlier by Reuters. In an order on Monday, Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín writes that the settlement will provide “meaningful relief,” offering authors around $3,000 for each book allegedly pirated by Anthropic. The $1.5 billion settlement is the “largest known copyright recovery in history,” according to the law firm representing the plaintiffs. A group of authors — Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber, and Kirk Wallace Johnson — first filed a copyright lawsuit against Anthropic in 2024. While the now-retired Judge William Alsup granted Anthropic a partial victory last year, he approved a separate class action lawsuit claiming the company engaged in the “Napster-style downloading of millions of works.” Anthropic agreed to a $1.5 billion settlement in September 2025, to which Judge Alsup later granted preliminary approval. “We are pleased that more than 91% of authors and publishers covered by the settlement have claimed their share of the payment,” Anthropic general counsel Aparna Sridhar tells Reuters. “We’re looking forward ​to bringing this matter to a close.” Anthropic is still facing copyright lawsuits from Chicken Soup for the Soul and several other authors who argue that $3,000 per book isn’t enough.

articles.title: No GPS required: Ukrainian 11th-grader creates AI drone navigation system
articles.summary: GPS jamming is one of modern drone warfare's biggest headaches — a Ukrainian 11th-grader just built an AI guidance system that doesn't need satellites at all
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

Ukrainian teenager develops drone autopilot capable of operating without GPS signals

11th-grade student Yaroslav Sheiko receives Ukraine's presidential award for drone innovations

Artificial intelligence powers the student's GPS-independent drone navigation technology

A Ukrainian high school student has developed drone technology capable of guiding unmanned aircraft without depending on satellite navigation systems.

Yaroslav Sheiko, an 11th-grade pupil from Poltava, received the presidential distinction known as "The Future of Ukraine" for his engineering achievements.

His work includes an artificial intelligence-powered flight control system and optical-electronic stabilization technology designed for unmanned aerial vehicles.

Sheiko's main innovation involves an autonomous guidance system that allows drones to reach designated destinations without relying on conventional satellite positioning signals.

The technology is designed to help unmanned aircraft maintain their intended flight paths when GPS and other global navigation services become unavailable.

According to information released by Poltava's municipal education department, the student has been developing engineering solutions for unmanned aerial vehicles.

His navigation system enables an aircraft to independently approach a location selected by its operator while flying relatively close to the ground.

This capability addresses a major difficulty facing drone operators when electronic interference disrupts satellite navigation signals during flight.

GPS jamming and spoofing can interfere with conventional navigation equipment, potentially preventing aircraft from maintaining accurate positioning.

Sheiko's work also includes optical-electronic stabilization equipment incorporating artificial intelligence for improved drone control and navigation.

Such equipment can help maintain stable observations and support guidance when conventional satellite-based positioning becomes unreliable.

However, there is no information on the precise sensors, algorithms, or computational hardware powering his navigation system.

Details about its operational testing, navigation accuracy, maximum range, and performance under different environmental conditions have also not been disclosed.

Without further technical details, it remains difficult to determine how his invention compares with existing GPS-independent navigation systems.

Nevertheless, receiving national recognition while still attending secondary school is a major achievement for the young Ukrainian engineer.

Presidential award follows several international science competition victories

The "The Future of Ukraine" distinction adds another achievement to Sheiko's growing record of recognition in engineering and scientific competitions.

He has previously received presidential scholarships on two occasions, recognizing his performance and contributions to scientific research.

The student has also secured first place twice in nationwide competitions organized by Ukraine's Junior Academy of Sciences.

His entries competed within the aerospace and defense technology category, focusing on engineering developments relevant to unmanned systems.

International competitions have also featured his inventions, including the INOVA 2025 International Inventions Show, where he secured a gold medal.

He additionally received a silver medal in the 2025 Hackathon, adding another international achievement to his academic record.

His latest presidential award recognizes his contributions to drone engineering, particularly developments involving autonomous navigation and electronic stabilization.

Ukraine's continuing efforts to maintain drone operations despite electronic interference have also encouraged interest in alternative communication technologies.

The country has been exploring alternatives to Starlink for maintaining drone communications when satellite connectivity becomes unavailable during military operations.

It recently reportedly combined airborne relay systems with Israeli-Italian satellite communications technology to provide alternative links for unmanned aircraft.

While these systems maintain communication with operators, Sheiko's invention addresses another challenge by allowing drones to navigate without GPS signals.

articles.title: JPMorgan Sees $450 Billion AI Debt Blitz in 2027 Before Plateau
articles.summary: Companies will tap public high-grade debt markets for $450 billion next year to finance their artificial intelligence-related capital expenditures, even as a...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Companies will tap public high-grade debt markets for $450 billion next year to finance their artificial intelligence-related capital expenditures, even as a growth plateau looms for the burgeoning industry further down the road, according to analysts at JPMorgan Chase & Co.

The financing would be an increase from the $368 billion of global investment grade bond issuance for AI-focused companies this year, according to the bank.

Overall, AI-related capital spending will nearly double to $1.4 trillion in 2027 before leveling off in the following year, strategists led by Tarek Hamid and Nathaniel Rosenbaum wrote.

The strategists expect spending growth to slow sharply in 2028 as the industry settles into a steady run rate — a trend potentially foreshadowed by cautious commentary from Asian tech giants including Tencent and Alibaba.

"Due to the deceleration in overall industry growth rates, there will be a quarter in late 2027 or early 2028 when the outlook for next quarter's capital spending will be basically flat," the strategists wrote. "Whether the market reacts positively or negatively to that is anyone's guess."

The shift is set to create a more predictable debt supply for credit markets even as flat spending growth risks unsettling investor sentiment, the strategists said.

The bank expects the AI industry to build 151 gigawatts of data center capacity at a cost of $7 trillion between 2027 and 2031. Since most data center projects take multiple years to build and raise capital upfront, much of 2027's buildout is already paid for, meaning "funding in 2027 is really for 2028," they wrote.

In addition to the investment-grade debt, the bank expects companies to raise $65 billion through leveraged finance and $25 billion to $35 billion in securitized products in 2027.

With debt markets approaching their capacity limits at that scale, cash-rich hyperscalers are seen carrying more of the equity load, requiring $2.9 trillion of equity invested in the sector over the next five years, largely from organic cash flow.

At the same time, the type of asset being financed is shifting from physical data centers toward compute hardware.

"The mix of AI accelerator financing is likely to increase dramatically across public and private markets. By 2031, GPU financing needs could exceed power shell financing needs by a factor of four," the strategists wrote.

articles.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and 'key man' risks | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The credit rating agency may lower Nvidia's credit rating to AA-, the fourth-highest rating.
articles.body:
S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.

Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement .

The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported .

A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

articles.title: SoftBank Credit Risk Tops 500 Basis Points as AI Worries Mount
articles.summary: SoftBank Group Corp.’s credit risk surged above 500 basis points for the first time in about four years, raising the prospect of even higher funding costs as...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- SoftBank Group Corp.'s credit risk surged above 500 basis points for the first time in about four years, raising the prospect of even higher funding costs as the company presses ahead with massive investments in artificial intelligence.

SoftBank's five-year credit-default swap rose to 516 basis points as of 6:30 a.m. in Tokyo, the highest since October 2022, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The spread on a dollar bond it sold in September with a 9.75% coupon, the highest ever for one of its dollar notes, has widened about 40% since issuance to about 644 basis points.

The deterioration comes as the AI stock trade reverses, raising questions about the future valuation of OpenAI, in which SoftBank has invested $64.6 billion, and its ability to recoup that investment. Wider bond spreads could also make future issuance and refinancing more expensive.

"The broadening of the AI business isn't going to change, but monetization will take longer," said Masahito Sugawara, a senior strategist at Daiwa Securities Co. For AI firms relying on future cash flows to repay debt, delays in monetization could complicate refinancing and "lead investors to demand wider spreads," he said.

SoftBank's financial burden is already growing. Finance costs in the July-September quarter rose 2.6 times from a year earlier to ¥461.9 billion ($2.9 billion). It raised about ¥9 trillion during the quarter.

S&P Global Ratings said this month that key metrics were approaching the tolerance limits for its rating on SoftBank. It estimated the loan-to-value ratio has risen above 30%, approaching its 35% threshold for considering a downgrade.

Anthropic PBC shares fell below their initial public offering price less than four sessions after their record-setting debut. OpenAI has ruled out an IPO this year, adding uncertainty over the eventual valuation and monetization of SoftBank's massive investment.

articles.title: A BITS Pilani alumnus from UP quit his high-paying Microsoft job to build a Bengaluru-based AI startup, missing Rs 15 lakh voluntary exit offer by just a month; his venture joins OpenAI's partner network
articles.summary: A month can make all the difference between walking away with a Rs 15 lakh payout and leaving with nothing.
articles.body: A month can make all the difference between walking away with a Rs 15 lakh payout and leaving with nothing. But for a former Microsoft employee, missing out on the money has not changed his mind about quitting the tech giant. Atishay Jain, a BITS Pilani alumnus from Baraut in Uttar Pradesh, quit his high-paying job at Microsoft last month to pursue his entrepreneurial ambitions and build his own AI company. However, just a month after his exit, Microsoft reportedly introduced a voluntary exit offer that could have fetched him approximately Rs 15 lakh had he stayed on a little longer.In a LinkedIn post, Jain reflected on the timing of his resignation, writing, "I just missed out on ~Rs 15 lakh by quitting one month too early." He acknowledged that the amount was not insignificant, especially considering that he had already made up his mind to leave the company. "Rs 15 LAKH. For leaving a job I'd already decided to leave," he wrote.While the missed payout could have been a reason to second-guess his decision, Jain said he had no intention of looking back. "Does it sting? Oh yes. Do I regret leaving? Not for a second," he wrote. Jain, who describes himself as a former Microsoft and Nutanix employee, said his first month working full-time on his venture, ScaleWorks AI, had already brought three developments worth celebrating.The Bengaluru-based company, which positions itself as an AI transformation partner helping businesses work smarter and scale faster, became an official member of the OpenAI Partner Network. Jain also said he was accepted into Toptal, a global network of freelance professionals that describes its talent pool as representing the top 3% of applicants. More importantly, leaving his full-time job gave him the freedom to devote all his attention to building his company.Reflecting on what he gained by leaving early, Jain posed a question that summed up his decision: "So, did I lose Rs 15 lakh by leaving a month early, or gain a month of building something that could change many lives? I guess only time will tell." articles.summary:
That’s gotta complete someone’s bingo card. As Aftermath points out, N3on was a fitting target — he’d previously used AI to create fake streams of himself, and “starred” in an AI movie.
